content_title: 2 cases of dengue fever confirmed in Citrus County
content: CITRUS COUNTY, Fla. — The Florida Department of Health in Citrus County reported Monday two confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue fever. DOH-Citrus and Citrus County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts. Dengue can present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash. Usually, there are no respiratory symptoms. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 15 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue fever is not contagious, but is transmitted by the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. DOH-Citrus reminds residents of ways to avoid mosquito bites. They include: - Wear protective clothing to prevent mosquito bites. Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants. - Apply insect repellents that are registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to exposed skin and clothing. When used as directed, EPA-registered insect repellents are proven safe and effective, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women. - Control mosquitoes inside and outside. Repair damaged screening on windows, doors, porches, and patios. Drain water from garbage cans, buckets, pool covers, coolers, toys, flowerpots, or any other containers where sprinkler or rainwater has collected

content_title: Florida Sees Increase in Locally Acquired Dengue Fever Cases
content: Gabriela Arevalo Fri, October 16, 2026 at 3:45 PM UTC 0 (bymuratdeniz / Getty Images) Florida is in the middle of a tropical disease outbreak that has surpassed both recent and historical records due to its severity, with one part of the Sunshine State being particularly hit by dengue fever. Related: Recall Expanded for Berries Sold at Walmart, Trader Joe’s, Publix Due to E. Coli Risk As of the latest report issued by state health officials, Florida saw an additional 72 cases of locally acquired dengue fever during the week of October 4 through 10 . “In 2026, 368 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from eight counties,” reads the report, noting that 26 cases of international travel-associated dengue were reported during the same time frame, bringing the year’s total of international travel-associated dengue to 288 cases. Most international travel-associated cases involved travel to Cuba (240), followed by eight cases linked to travel to Colombia, seven cases connected to travel to Nicaragua, and six cases related to travel to India. “In 2026, 368 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported in Broward, Hillsborough (310), Miami-Dade (9), Orange (5), Palm Beach, Pasco (4), Pinellas (37), and Polk [counties] with onset in July (21), August (159), and September (188),” says the report. Related: Meat Recall Issued for Beef, Pork, and More Nationwide: ‘Unsafe to Eat’ Per the Associated Press , this year’s outbreak is the highest for any state “since at least the 1940s,” based on medical journals and historical state health department information. According to Coral Springs News , an 80-year-old person died of “dengue infection” accompanied by multi-organ failure and septic shock in Hillsborough County, where Tampa is located. Workers in the region are spraying to diminish the mosquito population. Related: FDA Issues Nationwide Recall of Millions of Eye Drops–Find Out if You’re Affected Dengue fever is spread through mosquitoes in warm-weather regions like Florida, though historically most cases in the United States originate from international travel. Symptoms of dengue are similar to the flu, including high fever, headache, vomiting, and swollen glands, according to the Mayo Clinic . It’s also called breakbone fever due to the muscle, bone, or joint pain it can cause. Most people recover from dengue in one to two weeks, but may feel tired for several weeks after the illness. content_title: Dengue fever: why symptoms can worsen even after the fever subsides
content: Dengue fever: why symptoms can worsen even after the fever subsides Dengue often begins with fever, headache and body pain, but warning signs of severe infection can emerge as the temperature drops. A falling fever is usually seen as a sign of recovery, but in dengue patients, it can sometimes mark the beginning of a more dangerous phase of the illness. Health experts warn that severe dengue may develop as the fever subsides, making it important to monitor symptoms even when body temperature starts returning to normal. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. It is common in tropical and subtropical regions, including India, and mosquito activity often increases during and after rainy periods when stagnant water creates breeding sites. What Are the Early Symptoms of Dengue? Symptoms usually appear four to 10 days after an infected mosquito bite. Common signs include sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, and skin rash. Some infected people may experience mild symptoms or no symptoms at all. Because dengue symptoms can resemble those of other infections, medical evaluation and appropriate testing are important. A fever alone cannot confirm whether someone has dengue. Why Can Dengue Become Dangerous After the Fever Drops? The critical phase of dengue can occur around three to seven days after symptoms begin, often when the fever starts to subside. During this period, some patients can develop complications involving fluid leakage from blood vessels, severe bleeding or organ damage. A reduction in temperature does not necessarily mean the infection is resolving safely. Warning signs that require immediate medical attention include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, rapid breathing, unusual restlessness, and extreme weakness. Pale or cold skin can also signal a serious complication. How Is Dengue Treated? There is no specific antiviral medicine that cures dengue. Treatment generally focuses on managing symptoms, maintaining adequate fluid intake and monitoring the patient for complications. People who suspect they have dengue should seek medical advice rather than self-medicate. Paracetamol may be used for fever or pain when appropriate, but aspirin and ibuprofen should be avoided in suspected dengue because they can increase the risk of bleeding. Antibiotics do not treat dengue because it is caused by a virus. Simple Steps to Prevent Dengue Preventing mosquito bites and eliminating breeding sites are central to dengue control. Health authorities recommend the following measures: - Empty and clean water containers, coolers, and flowerpot trays regularly. - Cover water-storage tanks and discard objects that collect rainwater. - Use mosquito repellents according to label instructions. - Wear clothing that covers the arms and legs. - Install window screens and use mosquito nets when needed. The mosquitoes that transmit dengue are active during the day, so protection should not be limited to nighttime. Community participation in removing stagnant water can also reduce mosquito breeding around homes and workplaces
